---
title: "Sensitivity analysis with fect and HonestDiDFEct"
author: "Ziyi Liu"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110)
options(digits = 3)
```

A placebo test in **fect** holds out the last pre-treatment periods and
estimates effects there, where there should be no effect. `fect_sens()` uses
these placebo coefficients as a benchmark for how far parallel trends could fail
after treatment. It reports a robust confidence set for the treatment effect at
each degree of failure you allow. `fect_sens()` calls **HonestDiDFEct** for the
computation. You need both packages.

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("fect")
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("lzy318/HonestDiDFEct")
```

## Fit fect with placebo periods

The example is Hainmueller and Hangartner (2019), who study the effect of
indirect versus direct democracy on naturalization rates in Swiss
municipalities. The data come with **fect** as `hh2019`. The outcome
`nat_rate_ord` is the naturalization rate, and effects are in percentage points.

```{r fit, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, results="hide"}
library(fect)
data(hh2019)
out <- fect(nat_rate_ord ~ indirect, data = hh2019, index = c("bfs", "year"),
            method = "fe", se = TRUE,
            placeboTest = TRUE, placebo.period = c(-2, 0),
            parallel = FALSE, seed = 1234)
```

In **fect**, s = 1 is the first treated period and s = 0 is the last untreated
one. `placebo.period = c(-2, 0)` holds out s = -2, -1 and 0. **fect** imputes the
untreated outcome in these periods in the same way as after treatment.

```{r coefficients}
round(out$est.att[as.character(-2:6), c("ATT", "S.E.", "count")], 3)
round(diff(out$est.att[as.character(-2:0), "ATT"]), 3)
```

The first three rows are the placebo coefficients, and the last line gives the
changes between them. The number of treated units in `count` drops after s = 4.
This tutorial uses s = 1 to 4.

## Run the sensitivity analysis

```{r sens, message=FALSE}
out <- fect_sens(out, post.periods = 1:4,
                 Mbarvec = c(0, 0.5, 1), periodMbarvec = c(0, 0.5),
                 Mvec = c(0, 0.1, 0.2), periodMvec = c(0, 0.1))
```

`fect_sens()` applies two restrictions to the violation, the bias that the
failure of parallel trends adds to the estimate at each s. The
relative-magnitudes restriction (RM) bounds each change in the violation after
s = 0 by `Mbar` times the largest change between consecutive placebo periods.
That largest change is 0.23 here, from s = -2 to s = -1. The smoothness
restriction (SD) bounds the change in the slope of the violation from one period
to the next by `M`, in percentage points. The `Delta` column below shows them as
`DeltaRM` and `DeltaSD`.

Always pass `post.periods`, because its default fails. It must start at 1 and
have no gaps. `Mbarvec` and `Mvec` hold the values of `Mbar` and `M` for the
average effect, and `periodMbarvec` and `periodMvec` hold the values for each
period. Do not set a period vector to `NULL`, because that also drops the results
for the average effect. The fit and this call take a few minutes. Each value and
each post-treatment period adds run time.

## Read the average effect

```{r average}
as.data.frame(out$sensitivity.rm$original)
as.data.frame(out$sensitivity.rm$results)
plot(out, type = "sens", restrict = "rm", main = "Relative magnitudes")
```

`out$sensitivity.rm` holds the RM results, and `out$sensitivity.smooth` holds the
SD results. The target is the average effect over s = 1 to 4, weighted by the
number of treated units. `C-LF` in the `method` column is the conditional
least-favorable hybrid, which `fect_sens()` uses for both restrictions.

The Original interval is the usual confidence interval, on the coefficients as
**fect** reports them. For the robust confidence sets, `fect_sens()` first
subtracts the coefficient at s = 0, 0.254 here, from every coefficient. At
`Mbar = 0` the violation stays at its level at s = 0. The center of the robust
confidence set then lies 0.254 below the center of the Original interval.

Zero is outside the robust confidence set at `Mbar = 0.5` and inside it at
`Mbar = 1`. So the estimate stays significantly positive if each change in the
violation after treatment is at most half of the largest placebo change. It does
not if a change can be as large as that placebo change.

```{r smooth}
as.data.frame(out$sensitivity.smooth$results)
plot(out, type = "sens", restrict = "sm", main = "Smoothness")
```

At `M = 0` the robust confidence set is wide and includes zero. The violation
then continues in a straight line, with the slope it has between s = -1 and
s = 0. Extending that slope adds the sampling error of the placebo coefficients
to the estimate.

## Read the effect in each period

```{r event-study}
plot(out, type = "sens_es", restrict = "rm", main = "Relative magnitudes",
     xlim = c(-5, 6), ylim = c(-2, 5))
```

The dots and thin lines are the coefficients and confidence intervals from
**fect**, with the placebo periods in orange. The colored bars are the robust
confidence sets for each period, with the same 0.254 subtracted. At `Mbar = 0`
each bar is centered 0.254 below its dot, and at `Mbar = 0.5` about as far. At
`Mbar = 0.5` the bars for s = 2 and 3 lie above zero, and the bars for s = 1 and
4 include zero. The gray bars at the bottom show the number of treated units.
`out$sensitivity.rm$periods` holds the numbers, and `restrict = "sm"` gives the
same plot for the smoothness restriction.

## Use your own fect run

`fect_sens()` needs a `fect()` run with `placeboTest = TRUE` and `se = TRUE`. The
placebo periods must be consecutive and end at s = 0, and you need at least two
of them. Covariates, unbalanced panels, and estimators such as `method = "ife"`
and `method = "gsynth"` work as long as placebo periods are used. A run with
`loo = TRUE` does not work, and the package stops with a message.

To use another confidence-set method, or to add a sign or monotonicity
restriction, call `createSensitivityResults()` or
`createSensitivityResults_relativeMagnitudes()` yourself.

Rambachan and Roth (2023) define the restrictions, and Chiu et al. (2026) adapt
them to the estimators in **fect**. For a cohort-level analysis under staggered
adoption, see [CohortHonestDiD](https://github.com/lzy318/CohortHonestDiD) and
Liu (2026).
